question: In the context of Caribbean constitutional law, which doctrine holds that Parliament cannot bind its successors, thereby ensuring legislative supremacy remains unfettered?
options: A. The doctrine of legitimate expectations
B. The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty
C. The doctrine of separation of powers
D. The doctrine of desuetude

question: Under the law of contract, which principle established in Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] confirms that an advertisement can constitute a binding unilateral offer?
options: A. An advertisement is always an invitation to treat and never an offer
B. A unilateral offer made to the world at large can be accepted by performance of the stipulated conditions
C. Acceptance of a unilateral offer requires express communication to the offeror
D. Consideration is not required in unilateral contracts

question: Which landmark Privy Council decision established that Caribbean death row prisoners who had been held for an inordinate period of time could successfully argue that execution would constitute inhuman punishment?
options: A. Boyce v The Queen [2004]
B. Pratt and Morgan v Attorney General of Jamaica [1993]
C. Matthew v State of Trinidad and Tobago [2004]
D. DPP v Mollison [2003]

question: In tort law, the neighbour principle articulated by Lord Atkin in Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] requires which two elements to establish a duty of care under the original formulation?
options: A. Proximity and reasonable foreseeability of harm to the claimant
B. Assumption of responsibility and reliance by the claimant
C. A pre-existing contractual relationship and direct physical contact
D. Foreseeability of the class of harm and voluntary assumption of risk

question: Under the CARICOM Treaty framework, which body possesses the exclusive original jurisdiction to determine disputes between Member States concerning the interpretation and application of the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas?
options: A. The Caribbean Court of Justice in its appellate jurisdiction
B. The Caribbean Court of Justice in its original jurisdiction
C. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights
D. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

question: Which equitable maxim was applied in Chappell v Times Newspapers [1975] to refuse an injunction to employees who had breached their employment contracts, reflecting the principle that equity will not assist those who have not acted equitably?
options: A. Equity follows the law
B. He who comes to equity must come with clean hands
C. Delay defeats equity
D. Equity looks to the intent rather than the form

question: In criminal law, the M'Naghten Rules [1843] establish that a successful defence of insanity requires proof that at the time of committing the act, the accused was labouring under such a defect of reason from disease of the mind that he did not know:
options: A. Either that the act was physically wrong or that it was legally prohibited
B. The nature and quality of the act, or if he did know it, that he did not know what he was doing was wrong
C. The consequences of his actions or was unable to form the requisite mens rea
D. That society condemned the act or lacked the capacity to control his impulses

question: The rule in Rylands v Fletcher [1868] imposes strict liability where a person brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes. Which subsequent case significantly restricted its application by requiring the use to be 'non-natural'?
options: A. Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather [1994]
B. Read v J Lyons & Co [1947]
C. Transco plc v Stockport MBC [2003]
D. Goldman v Hargrave [1967]

question: Under the law of evidence in Commonwealth Caribbean jurisdictions, the principle of res gestae as an exception to the hearsay rule permits admission of statements made contemporaneously with an event. Which case best illustrates the 'startling event' limb of this exception?
options: A. R v Andrews [1987]
B. Myers v DPP [1965]
C. Sparks v R [1964]
D. Ratten v R [1972]

question: In constitutional law, the concept of 'constitutional entrenchment' means that certain provisions:
options: A. Can only be amended by a simple parliamentary majority following a public petition
B. Require a special majority in Parliament and sometimes a referendum for amendment
C. Are permanently unalterable and cannot be changed under any circumstances
D. Are suspended automatically during a state of emergency declared by the executive

question: Which doctrine in administrative law prevents a public authority from exercising its discretionary power for an improper purpose, as illustrated in Padfield v Minister of Agriculture [1968]?
options: A. The doctrine of proportionality
B. The ultra vires doctrine in its substantive sense
C. The doctrine of legitimate expectations
D. The Wednesbury unreasonableness principle

question: In the law of contract, the concept of promissory estoppel, developed in Central London Property Trust Ltd v High Trees House Ltd [1947], operates as:
options: A. A cause of action enabling a promisee to sue on a gratuitous promise
B. A shield preventing the promisor from enforcing strict legal rights where it would be inequitable to do so
C. A sword allowing recovery of damages for detrimental reliance on a promise
D. A doctrine requiring consideration to be executory rather than executed

question: Under Caribbean human rights jurisprudence, which case established that mandatory sentencing provisions that remove judicial discretion may violate constitutional protections against inhuman or degrading punishment?
options: A. Watson v The Queen [2004]
B. Reyes v The Queen [2002]
C. Fox v The Queen [2002]
D. Balkissoon Roodal v The State [2003]

question: The tort of private nuisance protects against unlawful interference with the use and enjoyment of land. The House of Lords in Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd [1997] confirmed that only which category of person may sue in private nuisance?
options: A. Any person physically present on the land at the time of the interference
B. A person with a proprietary or possessory interest in the affected land
C. Any member of the household of the landowner who suffers personal injury
D. Any person who can demonstrate special damage arising from the interference

question: In criminal law, the Accessories and Abettors Act principle distinguishes between a principal and an accessory. Which rule from R v Jogee [2016] reformed the law regarding joint enterprise liability?
options: A. Foresight of a possibility that a principal might commit an offence is sufficient for secondary liability
B. The mere presence of the accessory at the scene of the crime automatically establishes liability
C. Parasitic accessory liability was abolished and secondary liability now requires intentional assistance or encouragement
D. An accessory is only liable if he has the same mens rea as the principal offender
